newsitem.title: USA: Minor Metals cobalt criticism legitimate - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals cobalt criticism legitimate - dealers.

text.p: Minor Metals Inc's latest cobalt-coated brickbat thrown at the U.S. Defense National Stockpile Center concerning the Center's new assaying policy is justified, according to traders and consumers in the cobalt market.
In its latest sale of cobalt, the Stockpile had an independent assayer sample and analyze 25 percent of the material for sale, but retained its no-warranty/no-guarantee policy.

Minor Metals submitted a bid with an added provision to sample the remaining material at its own expense and wanted a right to a refund if the material was found to be below the specifications of the sample. The bid was rejected by the Stockpile.
In an open letter to the Stockpile, Minor Metals criticized the new Stockpile provisions, saying that traders bear an inordinate risk if the material doesn't conform to the assayer's analysis.
"There is...no quality protection whatsoever for material which is found to contain some cobalt but less than the cobalt content stated in the solicitation," the letter said.

"The Stockpile is doing a commercially decent job," said one cobalt trader. "But I would appreciate 100 percent assaying. We take a lot of risk in the market. If the material we sell isn't what the assay says it is, it costs us money."

"We hope the DNSC will appreciate that practically no buyer (consumer, producer, trader) in the world is prepared to buy cobalt metal without having a quality guarantee or, as a minimum, having the ability to sample the material first," Minor Metals' letter said.
"He's absolutely right," another trader said. "That's why we came up with alternatives to sourcing our metal from the stockpile."
But other dealers say that's the risk one takes when buys from the government. It's also one reason that government metal is well below market prices.

"Twenty-five percent sampling is reasonable," another source said. "One hundred percent would be better, but that comes at an additional expense. You can reduce that risk (by buying) in the open market, but you'd be paying a higher price."

One consumer noted that traders tend to be more vulnerable to quality risks than consumers. "A consumer bears 100 percent of the risk himself," he said. "He doesn't have to pass that risk along to a customer.
"If the material is not up to spec, the trader is in the position of having to offer a lower price than what he paid," he added. "That's the risk."
The Stockpile solicitation does include provisions for filing disputes in writing to the contracting officer, at which point the Stockpile will seek an "amicable" solution.
"We will entertain any claim from anybody for any reason," said Essie Schloss, the Stockpile's general counsel. "We can't promise to make everyone happy. But we'll certainly try."
The assaying issue isn't likely to go away any time soon. The Stockpile is in the process of assembling a final solicitation for a 1.5-million-lb negotiated bid offering scheduled for August 29.

At an industry meeting convened by the Stockpile, the assaying issue was discussed at length. "Some people made it clear that they wanted 100 percent sampling," said a government official. "Certainly that's something we'll consider in the future."
